title: The Electronic Schrödinger Equation
description: Born-Oppenheimer, the molecular Hamiltonian, and why nuclei sit still

concepts.title: The Molecular Hamiltonian
concepts.contentHtml:
A molecule of N electrons and M nuclei is described by a Schrödinger equation whose Hamiltonian contains five terms: nuclear kinetic energy, electron kinetic energy, electron-nucleus attraction, electron-electron repulsion, and nucleus-nucleus repulsion. The full Coulomb Hamiltonian is conceptually simple but contains every bit of chemistry — bond strengths, geometries, reaction barriers, spectra — and is essentially impossible to solve exactly for anything bigger than H₂⁺.

The reason is the electron-electron term 1/r_ij. It couples every pair of electrons, so the wavefunction cannot factor into a product of one-electron pieces. Solving exactly means working in a space whose dimension scales as 3N for the wavefunction's coordinates — for a molecule of just 20 electrons, a 60-dimensional integral. The exponential wall of dimensionality is the central problem of quantum chemistry.

Every method you'll meet — Hartree-Fock, MP2, coupled cluster, DFT — is a different strategy for sneaking around this wall. None solve the equation exactly; each makes a controlled approximation and tracks the error.

concepts.title: Born-Oppenheimer: Freezing the Nuclei
concepts.contentHtml:
Nuclei are at least 1836 times heavier than electrons (the proton-to-electron mass ratio). Electrons therefore move on a much faster timescale; on the electron's clock, nuclei are essentially stationary. This is the Born-Oppenheimer (BO) approximation: separate the nuclear and electronic problems by treating nuclear positions R as fixed parameters in the electronic Schrödinger equation.

The result is the electronic Hamiltonian Ĥ_elec(R), which depends on nuclear coordinates parametrically. Solving it at a single geometry gives an electronic energy E_elec(R); mapping over many geometries produces a potential energy surface (PES). Equilibrium structures are minima on the PES; transition states are first-order saddle points; reaction barriers are PES height differences.

BO breaks down where electronic states get close in energy — conical intersections, photochemistry, ultrafast nonadiabatic dynamics, the Jahn-Teller effect. In those cases you need surface-hopping or fully nonadiabatic methods. For 95% of ground-state chemistry, BO is exact for all practical purposes; the residual error is well below typical method error.

concepts.title: Antisymmetry and Slater Determinants
concepts.contentHtml:
Electrons are fermions: the total wavefunction must change sign under exchange of any two electrons. A simple product (Hartree product) of one-electron orbitals is not antisymmetric — swapping two coordinates leaves it unchanged. The fix is the Slater determinant, which builds antisymmetry directly into the wavefunction by construction:

For N electrons in spin-orbitals χ_1, χ_2, ..., χ_N, the determinant of an N×N matrix automatically gives a sign change on row swaps (i.e., electron exchange) and produces zero whenever two electrons share the same spin-orbital — the Pauli exclusion principle falling out of pure linear algebra.

One Slater determinant is the simplest antisymmetric ansatz; this is what Hartree-Fock uses. The exact wavefunction generally needs an infinite linear combination of determinants, which is what configuration interaction (CI), coupled cluster (CC), and other post-HF methods build. The cost of antisymmetry is the exchange interaction — a non-classical correction to electron-electron repulsion that emerges purely from the determinant structure, not from any new physical force. It will reappear as the K̂ exchange operator in the next lesson.

title: Hartree-Fock and the Self-Consistent Field
description: Variational principle, the Fock operator, and SCF iteration

concepts.title: Variational Principle and the HF Ansatz
concepts.contentHtml:
The variational principle says that any trial wavefunction's energy expectation value is an upper bound on the true ground-state energy. Minimize the trial energy over the parameter space and you'll get the best wavefunction within that family — and a guaranteed-too-high energy.

Hartree-Fock (HF) takes the simplest antisymmetric ansatz: a single Slater determinant. The variational parameters are the orbitals themselves, expanded in a basis (more on basis sets next lesson). Minimizing <Ψ|Ĥ|Ψ> subject to orbital orthonormality yields the Hartree-Fock equations — eigenvalue equations for the orbitals.

Each electron in HF moves in the average field of all the others — a mean-field approximation. The instantaneous correlation between electrons (one moves, others get out of the way) is not captured. Whatever HF misses is, by definition, the correlation energy: E_corr = E_exact − E_HF. For a closed-shell molecule near equilibrium, HF recovers about 99% of the total energy but misses ~1%, and that 1% is exactly the chemistry.

concepts.title: The Fock Operator: Coulomb and Exchange
concepts.contentHtml:
The HF orbitals satisfy F̂ φ_i = ε_i φ_i, where F̂ is the Fock operator. It contains the one-electron core Hamiltonian (kinetic + nuclear attraction) plus two two-electron terms: the Coulomb operator Ĵ (classical electron-electron repulsion averaged over orbitals) and the exchange operator K̂ (a non-local quantum correction that emerges from the determinant antisymmetry).

Exchange is purely a consequence of fermion statistics — it has no classical analog. For same-spin electrons, exchange reduces the apparent repulsion (the Fermi hole — same-spin electrons effectively avoid each other, lowering the energy by ~0.5-1 eV per pair). HF treats exchange exactly within the single-determinant ansatz; this is one of HF's strengths and a key reason hybrid DFT functionals like B3LYP reintroduce a fraction of HF exchange to fix self-interaction error.

The catch: F̂ depends on the orbitals it's solving for, since Ĵ and K̂ are built from the occupied orbitals. The equations are nonlinear. You can't just diagonalize once — you have to iterate to self-consistency, which is what the SCF loop in the next concept does.

concepts.title: SCF Iteration and Roothaan Equations
concepts.contentHtml:
The procedure is the self-consistent field (SCF) loop. (1) Guess a set of orbitals (typically from a cheaper calculation or a superposition of atomic densities). (2) Build the Fock matrix from those orbitals. (3) Diagonalize to get new orbitals and energies. (4) Compare the density to the previous iteration. If converged (typically <10⁻⁶ in density), stop; otherwise loop.

In practice we expand orbitals in a finite basis: φ_i = Σ_μ C_μi χ_μ. The HF equations become the matrix Roothaan-Hall equations FC = SCε, a generalized eigenvalue problem in the basis-function coefficients. S is the overlap matrix (basis functions on different atoms aren't orthogonal).

SCF convergence isn't guaranteed and can fail spectacularly on transition metals, biradicals, or near-degeneracies. Modern codes use DIIS (Direct Inversion of the Iterative Subspace, Pulay 1980) — extrapolating from previous Fock matrices to accelerate convergence. Cost scales as O(N⁴) in basis size for canonical HF (though linear-scaling variants exist for huge systems). HF is rarely the final answer in modern work, but it's the foundation that nearly every other method builds on.

title: Basis Sets: STO, GTO, Pople, and Dunning
description: How orbitals are represented numerically — and the cost of being incomplete

concepts.title: STO vs GTO and the Contraction Trick
concepts.contentHtml:
The natural choice for an atomic orbital is a Slater-type orbital (STO) with the form r^(n-1) exp(-ζr), which has the correct cusp at the nucleus and the correct exponential decay at infinity. STOs match hydrogen-like orbitals exactly. The problem: the four-center two-electron integrals (μν|λσ) involving STOs centered on different atoms have no closed form. They require expensive numerical integration.

S. F. Boys (1950) noticed something pivotal: products of Gaussian-type orbitals (GTOs) exp(-αr²) centered on different atoms give a Gaussian centered between them. All four-center integrals reduce to closed-form expressions. The cost: a single Gaussian has the wrong cusp (smooth at the nucleus, not pointed) and decays too fast.

The fix is a contracted GTO: a fixed linear combination of several primitive Gaussians designed to mimic an STO. STO-3G fits an STO with three Gaussians per atomic orbital — fast, but minimal quality. Modern Pople and correlation-consistent bases use larger contractions tuned for accuracy.
mathExpressions: \chi^\text{STO}(\mathbf{r}) = N r^{n-1} e^{-\zeta r} Y_{\ell m}
\chi^\text{GTO}(\mathbf{r}) = N x^{l_x} y^{l_y} z^{l_z} e^{-\alpha r^2}

concepts.title: Pople Basis Sets: 6-31G* and the Polarization Story
concepts.contentHtml:
The Pople nomenclature 6-31G* tells you the structure. "6" means inner-shell (core) orbitals are described by a single contracted GTO of 6 primitives. "31" means valence orbitals are split-valence: an inner contraction of 3 primitives and an outer contraction of 1 primitive — giving the basis flexibility to relax in different chemical environments.

The asterisks add polarization functions: 6-31G* (or 6-31G(d)) adds d-functions to heavy atoms; 6-31G** (or 6-31G(d,p)) adds p-functions to hydrogens too. Polarization functions let orbitals deform from spherical symmetry — essential for any geometry where atomic orbitals shouldn't be perfectly atom-centered (i.e., almost all of chemistry).

The plus signs add diffuse functions (small exponents, large spatial extent): 6-31+G* on heavy atoms, 6-31++G* on H too. Diffuse functions are critical for anions, weakly bound complexes, hydrogen bonding, and excited states. Skipping them on an anion is a classic beginner error — the energy can be off by tens of kJ/mol.
mathExpressions: \text{6-31G(d,p)}: \text{ split-valence + d on heavy atoms + p on H}
\text{6-311++G(d,p)}: \text{ triple-zeta + diffuse on H and heavy + polarization}

concepts.title: Correlation-Consistent Bases and Extrapolation
concepts.contentHtml:
Dunning's correlation-consistent basis sets (cc-pVnZ, n = D, T, Q, 5, 6) are designed so that adding the next shell of functions recovers a roughly fixed fraction of the remaining correlation energy. They form a systematic ladder: cc-pVDZ → cc-pVTZ → cc-pVQZ → cc-pV5Z, with prefix "aug-" adding diffuse functions (aug-cc-pVTZ).

The key practical advantage: results extrapolate smoothly to the complete basis set (CBS) limit. The standard Helgaker formula E(n) = E_CBS + A·n^(-3) uses two or three points to estimate the infinite-basis answer. A typical workflow runs cc-pVTZ and cc-pVQZ, extrapolates, and quotes a CBS-limit energy — the basis-set error becomes a controlled, quantifiable quantity rather than a hidden bias.

Cost is steep: doubling the basis quadruples the time for HF, scales as N⁴ in basis size for HF and worse for post-HF methods (N⁵ for MP2, N⁷ for CCSD(T)). cc-pVQZ on a 50-atom organic molecule with CCSD(T) is at the edge of what's practical even in 2026. The choice of basis is rarely about "accuracy" alone — it's an accuracy-vs-cost trade you make on every calculation.
mathExpressions: E(n) = E_\text{CBS} + A n^{-3} \quad \text{(Helgaker extrapolation, } n = \text{cardinal number)}

title: Electron Correlation: MP2, CC, and the Gold Standard
description: Beyond mean field — perturbation theory, coupled cluster, and CCSD(T)

concepts.title: Møller-Plesset Perturbation Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
MP2 is the simplest practical post-HF correlation method. Treat the difference between the exact electronic Hamiltonian and the Fock operator as a perturbation, and apply Rayleigh-Schrödinger perturbation theory through second order. The result is a closed-form correction involving double-excitation integrals weighted by orbital-energy denominators.

MP2 typically recovers 80-90% of the correlation energy in a given basis at modest cost — formally O(N⁵), in practice often the cheapest route to chemical accuracy for organic molecules near equilibrium. With cc-pVTZ basis it's the entry-level workhorse for energies, geometries, and intermolecular interactions.

Where MP2 fails: stretched bonds, near-degeneracies, and any situation where a single Slater determinant is a poor reference (because perturbation theory blows up when the denominator ε_a + ε_b − ε_i − ε_j approaches zero). MP3 and MP4 add higher orders; the series doesn't always converge — for some systems MP4 is worse than MP2. Higher-order MP is rarely used now; coupled cluster has eaten its lunch.

concepts.title: Coupled Cluster: The Exponential Ansatz
concepts.contentHtml:
Coupled cluster (CC) writes the wavefunction as |Ψ⟩ = e^T̂ |Φ_0⟩, where T̂ is a sum of excitation operators and Φ_0 is the HF reference. Truncating T̂ to single and double excitations gives CCSD; including triples gives CCSDT. The exponential ensures size-consistency — the energy of two non-interacting fragments equals the sum of fragment energies — a property that truncated CI badly violates.

CCSD(T) — "the gold standard of quantum chemistry" — adds triples perturbatively (the parenthetical T) on top of CCSD. It typically reaches "chemical accuracy" (~1 kcal/mol, ~4 kJ/mol) for well-behaved closed-shell systems. Benchmarks like the W4 protocol use CCSD(T) with massive basis extrapolation as a reference standard against which everything else (DFT functionals, MP2, semi-empirical methods) is judged.

Cost scales as O(N⁷) for CCSD(T) — pushing it past ~30 atoms is heroic. Local correlation methods (DLPNO-CCSD(T), pioneered by Neese and coworkers in ORCA) exploit locality of correlation to achieve near-linear scaling, making CCSD(T)-quality results feasible on systems with 100+ atoms. This is one of the most important practical advances of the last fifteen years.

concepts.title: Configuration Interaction and CASSCF
concepts.contentHtml:
Configuration interaction (CI) expands the wavefunction as a linear combination of Slater determinants — the HF reference plus excited determinants. Truncated CI (CISD: singles + doubles) is cheaper than CC but loses size-consistency, which is a death blow for any chemistry involving fragmentation. Full CI (FCI) in a finite basis is the exact answer — but its cost scales factorially in the number of orbitals; FCI is feasible only for tiny systems (a few atoms in modest bases).

For molecules with strong static correlation — bond dissociation, biradicals, transition metals with near-degenerate d configurations — a single-reference treatment fails. CASSCF (Complete Active Space SCF) optimizes both the orbitals and the CI coefficients within a chosen active space of "chemically important" orbitals. A typical choice for ozone or a transition metal complex might be CAS(8,8): 8 electrons in 8 orbitals, FCI within that space.

CASSCF captures static correlation but misses dynamic correlation. The follow-up CASPT2 or NEVPT2 adds dynamic correlation perturbatively on the CASSCF reference. This is the standard recipe for excited states and challenging multireference ground states. Choosing the active space is the dark art — an experienced quantum chemist's hardest skill.
mathExpressions: \text{CAS}(n,m): \; n \text{ electrons in } m \text{ active orbitals}

title: Density Functional Theory: Hohenberg-Kohn and Kohn-Sham
description: Trading the wavefunction for the density — and why it works

concepts.title: The Hohenberg-Kohn Theorems
concepts.contentHtml:
Hohenberg and Kohn (1964) proved two existence theorems that recast quantum chemistry. HK1: the ground-state electron density ρ(r) uniquely determines the external potential (and hence the Hamiltonian, and hence everything). The wavefunction depends on 3N coordinates; the density depends on 3. If you can work with the density, you've collapsed the dimensionality of the problem.

HK2: there exists a universal energy functional E[ρ], with the property that the true ground-state density is the one that minimizes E[ρ], returning the true ground-state energy. The functional has parts you can write down (kinetic energy of non-interacting electrons, nuclear attraction, classical Coulomb repulsion of the density with itself) and a remainder — the exchange-correlation functional E_xc[ρ] — whose exact form is unknown.

HK is an existence proof: it tells you the functional exists but not what it is. Sixty years of DFT research is the search for accurate approximations to E_xc[ρ]. The remarkable thing is how well even crude approximations work in practice.

concepts.title: Kohn-Sham: Reintroducing Orbitals
concepts.contentHtml:
Pure density functionals struggle with the kinetic energy: the explicit kinetic energy functional of ρ alone (Thomas-Fermi) is very inaccurate. Kohn and Sham (1965) had a brilliant move: imagine a fictitious system of non-interacting electrons with the same density as the real interacting system. Write its kinetic energy T_s exactly using one-electron orbitals — the Kohn-Sham orbitals.

The KS equations look exactly like Hartree-Fock but with a different effective potential: kinetic + nuclear + Hartree (classical electron-electron) + v_xc(r) = δE_xc/δρ. The exchange-correlation potential bundles all the quantum many-body effects into a single multiplicative function (or, for hybrids, a combination of local and non-local terms).

Solve the KS equations self-consistently — same SCF loop as HF — and you get the density and energy. Cost is O(N³) for many implementations, vastly cheaper than CCSD(T)'s O(N⁷). DFT is the workhorse of practical quantum chemistry: 90%+ of papers in the field use it. KS orbitals are not the same as physical molecular orbitals — they're defined by a fictitious system — but they're often used as if they were, with mostly forgivable inaccuracy.

concepts.title: Why DFT Works (and Where It Doesn't)
concepts.contentHtml:
DFT consistently outperforms expectations. A method whose central object — E_xc[ρ] — is fundamentally unknown still delivers chemical accuracy on a vast range of systems. Why? Most of the difficult physics (kinetic energy, classical repulsion) is treated nearly exactly. Exchange-correlation is the residual ~10% of the energy, and even crude approximations capture it well enough.

But DFT is not a black box. Self-interaction error (SIE): a single electron in standard DFT spuriously interacts with itself through the Hartree term, an error not fully cancelled by approximate v_xc. SIE corrupts barrier heights, charge-transfer states, and odd-electron systems. Dispersion (van der Waals): standard local/semi-local functionals miss the long-range correlation that produces dispersion forces; an empirical correction (Grimme's D3 or D4) is now standard practice.

And DFT is not systematically improvable. With CCSD(T) you can run CCSDT, CCSDTQ, or extrapolate the basis — every step has a known direction of improvement. With DFT, B3LYP fails on a system; do you go to ωB97X-D, M06-2X, or PBE0? The answer is empirical. This is the great irony of DFT: it works astonishingly well on average and is the right tool for most jobs, but it is fundamentally non-systematic.
mathExpressions: E_\text{xc}[\rho] \approx 10\% \text{ of total energy, but contains nearly all the chemistry}

title: The Functional Zoo and Jacob's Ladder
description: LDA, GGA, meta-GGA, hybrids, double-hybrids — and which to actually use

concepts.title: Jacob's Ladder of Functionals
concepts.contentHtml:
John Perdew's Jacob's Ladder organizes density functionals by what local information they use. Rung 1, LDA (Local Density Approximation): E_xc depends only on the local density ρ(r), parameterized to match the homogeneous electron gas. Crude but surprisingly useful for solids; bad for atoms and molecules.

Rung 2, GGA (Generalized Gradient Approximation): adds ∇ρ. Examples: PBE (the default in solid-state physics), BLYP. Cures most of LDA's overbinding and is the cheapest workable choice for many tasks. Rung 3, meta-GGA: adds the kinetic-energy density τ(r). Examples: M06, SCAN. Better thermochemistry, better noncovalent interactions, more variation across functionals.

Rung 4, hybrids: mix in a fraction of exact (HF) exchange. B3LYP uses 20% HF exchange and is the most-cited functional in chemistry — for years the default in Gaussian. Rung 5, double-hybrids: hybrids plus a fraction of MP2-like correlation. B2PLYP, DSD-PBEP86. Each rung climbs in accuracy and cost; the right rung depends on what you need.

concepts.title: B3LYP, ωB97X-D, M06, PBE: Choosing a Functional
concepts.contentHtml:
B3LYP (1994) is the historical workhorse — three-parameter Becke exchange + Lee-Yang-Parr correlation + 20% HF exchange. Reasonable for organic thermochemistry near equilibrium. Bad for noncovalent interactions (no dispersion), poor on transition metals, and has known errors for charge-transfer states. Add D3(BJ) dispersion (B3LYP-D3BJ) and it improves dramatically.

ωB97X-D (Head-Gordon, 2008) is a range-separated hybrid: it switches from short-range DFT exchange to full HF exchange at long range, fixing self-interaction error for charge-transfer and Rydberg states. The "D" includes empirical dispersion. It's an excellent default for excited states, charge-transfer, and noncovalent complexes.

M06-2X (Truhlar, 2008) is heavily parameterized for thermochemistry, kinetics, and noncovalent interactions. PBE (Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof, 1996) is the GGA standard in solid-state and materials physics — non-empirical, robust, modest accuracy. SCAN (2015) is a non-empirical meta-GGA satisfying many exact constraints; an excellent default for systems where parameterized hybrids feel like cheating. The honest truth: there is no universal best functional. Benchmark on systems similar to yours, or trust someone else's benchmark.

concepts.title: Benchmarks: G2, GMTKN55, and Honesty
concepts.contentHtml:
How do you know if a functional is any good? You benchmark it. The classic G2/G3 set (Pople and Curtiss, 1990s) collects atomization energies, ionization potentials, and electron affinities for small molecules with high-level reference data. A method's mean absolute error on G2 was the standard quality metric for years.

The modern gold standard is GMTKN55 (Goerigk and Grimme, 2017): a database of 55 benchmark sets covering ~1,500 reaction energies and ~500 transition states across thermochemistry, kinetics, and noncovalent interactions. Reference values come from CCSD(T)/CBS calculations. Every major functional has been run on GMTKN55, and the leaderboard is the most reliable tool for choosing one.

The pattern that emerges: double-hybrids (DSD-BLYP, ωB97M(2)) sit at the top with mean absolute errors near 2-3 kcal/mol; hybrids (ωB97X-V, M06-2X-D3, B3LYP-D3) follow at 4-6 kcal/mol; meta-GGAs at 6-8 kcal/mol; GGAs at 8-12 kcal/mol; LDA brings up the rear. This rank order is robust enough to guide method selection — but always validate on your specific chemistry, because every functional has its blind spots.

title: Excited States: TDDFT, CASPT2, and Photochemistry
description: UV-Vis prediction, conical intersections, and the multireference frontier

concepts.title: TDDFT: Linear Response from a DFT Ground State
concepts.contentHtml:
Time-dependent DFT (TDDFT) generalizes ground-state DFT to time-dependent external potentials via the Runge-Gross theorem. In the linear response regime — where the perturbation is weak — solving the TDDFT equations reduces to a non-Hermitian eigenvalue problem (the Casida equations) that yields vertical excitation energies and oscillator strengths in a single calculation.

For most organic chromophores, TDDFT with a good range-separated hybrid (ωB97X-D, CAM-B3LYP) and a reasonable basis (def2-TZVP or aug-cc-pVDZ) gives UV-Vis spectra accurate to 0.2-0.4 eV — useful for assignment and trend prediction. The Tamm-Dancoff approximation (TDA) simplifies the equations by zeroing the B-block and is more robust for triplets, often used by default.

TDDFT's failure modes are well-known. Charge-transfer states: standard global hybrids hugely underestimate CT excitation energies; range-separated functionals fix this. Rydberg states: need diffuse functions and good asymptotic behavior of v_xc. Doubly excited states: missed entirely by linear-response TDDFT, since only single excitations enter the response. Conical intersections between S0 and S1: linear-response TDDFT produces a seam of the wrong dimensionality, breaking nonadiabatic dynamics in the most important region.

concepts.title: When Single Reference Fails: CASPT2 and NEVPT2
concepts.contentHtml:
For excited states with strong multireference character — open-shell singlets, biradicals, photochemical intermediates near conical intersections, transition metals with low-spin/high-spin near-degeneracy — TDDFT and CCSD(T) both break. The honest tool is multireference perturbation theory built on a CASSCF reference.

CASPT2 (Roos, 1990) and NEVPT2 (Angeli et al., 2001) add second-order dynamic correlation to a CASSCF wavefunction. CASPT2 is older and widely used but suffers from intruder states — perturbative denominators that go to zero — typically patched with a level shift. NEVPT2 is intruder-state free by construction (uses a different zeroth-order Hamiltonian) and is increasingly the default.

The bottleneck is choosing the active space. CAS(8,8) might be enough for a ketone n→π* state; a transition metal complex might demand CAS(14,14) or larger, and the cost grows factorially. Modern strategies include automated active space selection (AVAS, atomic valence active space) and methods like DMRG-CASSCF (density matrix renormalization group), which handles active spaces of 30+ orbitals — territory unreachable by traditional CI.

concepts.title: Conical Intersections and Nonadiabatic Dynamics
concepts.contentHtml:
The Born-Oppenheimer picture pictures separate, smooth potential energy surfaces. In photochemistry, surfaces touch — at conical intersections (CIs), where two electronic states become degenerate and the BO approximation fails completely. CIs are the funnels through which excited molecules rapidly (femtoseconds) transfer energy from electronic to nuclear motion: vision (rhodopsin), photosynthesis, DNA photoprotection, and singlet fission all proceed through CIs.

At a CI, two coordinates lift the degeneracy linearly: the gradient difference and the nonadiabatic coupling vectors. Locating CIs requires methods that treat both states on equal footing — SA-CASSCF (state-averaged CASSCF), MS-CASPT2, or SF-TDDFT (spin-flip). Standard TDDFT cannot reach a true CI between the ground state and an excited state.

Real photodynamics is nonadiabatic: nuclei evolve on multiple coupled surfaces. Trajectory surface hopping (Tully) propagates classical nuclei on one surface at a time but allows stochastic hops between surfaces governed by nonadiabatic coupling. Ab initio multiple spawning (AIMS) uses Gaussian wavepackets that branch at CIs. These methods, combined with on-the-fly CASSCF or CASPT2 forces, are how modern computational photochemistry actually predicts excited-state lifetimes and product ratios.

title: Geometries, Frequencies, and Thermochemistry
description: Optimization, transition states, and going from electronic energy to ΔG

concepts.title: Geometry Optimization
concepts.contentHtml:
A molecule's equilibrium geometry is a stationary point on the PES — gradient zero, Hessian positive-definite (a minimum). Optimization is iterative: at each step, evaluate the energy and its gradient (analytic gradients are essential — finite-difference is too expensive), step toward the predicted minimum using a quasi-Newton method (BFGS is the default), and repeat until the gradient drops below a threshold (typically 4·10⁻⁴ a.u. RMS in Gaussian's defaults).

Internal coordinates (bond lengths, angles, dihedrals) work much better than Cartesians for organic molecules — they decouple the slow modes (torsions) from the stiff modes (bond stretches). The redundant internal coordinate system (Pulay) is the standard choice in Gaussian, ORCA, and most modern codes.

The biggest hidden cost is the initial guess. A good starting geometry (from a force field, a related crystal structure, or a previous calculation) might converge in 10 steps; a bad guess might take 100 or fail entirely. Symmetric structures sit at saddle points and need symmetry-breaking perturbation. For floppy molecules, multiple conformers must be optimized separately — there's no single answer.

concepts.title: Vibrational Frequencies and Hessians
concepts.contentHtml:
At a stationary point, the mass-weighted Hessian diagonalizes into normal modes; its eigenvalues are ω². Real positive frequencies confirm a minimum; one imaginary frequency confirms a transition state (saddle point of index 1); two or more imaginary frequencies mean you're not at a useful stationary point. Always run frequencies after optimization — it's the only way to verify what you found.

Frequencies also let you compute thermochemical corrections. Within the rigid rotor / harmonic oscillator approximation, you get the zero-point energy (ZPE), the thermal correction to the enthalpy, and the entropy. Adding these to the electronic energy gives H, S, and G at any temperature — the quantities you need to compare with experiment (ΔG of reaction, equilibrium constants, activation energies).

Calculated frequencies are systematically too high (typically 3-5%) because the harmonic approximation neglects anharmonicity. Standard practice: scale frequencies by an empirical factor (e.g., 0.9614 for B3LYP/6-31G(d), tabulated in NIST CCCBDB) before comparing to IR spectra. For ZPE, a separate scale factor is used. Anharmonic corrections via VPT2 (vibrational perturbation theory) are available but rarely necessary for routine work.
mathExpressions: \omega_i^2 = \text{eigenvalues of } \mathbf{H}_\text{mw}, \quad H_{\text{mw},ij} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{m_i m_j}} \frac{\partial^2 E}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}

concepts.title: Transition States and Reaction Paths
concepts.contentHtml:
A transition state (TS) is a saddle point of index 1: gradient zero, exactly one negative eigenvalue of the Hessian. Finding TSs is much harder than finding minima. QST2/QST3 (quadratic synchronous transit) interpolates between reactant and product to guess a TS. NEB (nudged elastic band) and string methods propagate a chain of images along the reaction path and converge to the minimum-energy path. The dimer method (Henkelman) walks uphill along the lowest mode without needing a product structure.

Once located, a TS is verified by (1) one imaginary frequency whose displacement vector matches the chemical motion, and (2) IRC (intrinsic reaction coordinate) tracking — the steepest-descent path from the TS in mass-weighted coordinates connecting reactant and product. Without an IRC check, you might be looking at a saddle point of the wrong reaction.

Activation energies from these calculations feed directly into transition state theory: the rate constant k(T) = (k_B T / h) exp(−ΔG‡/RT). With realistic functional + basis (e.g., ωB97X-D/def2-TZVP), absolute activation barriers are accurate to ~2-3 kcal/mol — enough to predict whether a reaction is fast or slow, and to rank competing pathways. For finer accuracy, single-point CCSD(T)/CBS on DFT-optimized geometries is the standard high-end recipe.
mathExpressions: k(T) = \frac{k_B T}{h} e^{-\Delta G^\ddagger / RT} \quad \text{(Eyring equation)}

title: Solvation and Software Practice
description: PCM, COSMO, QM/MM, and the codes you actually use — Gaussian, ORCA, Psi4

concepts.title: Implicit Solvation: PCM and COSMO
concepts.contentHtml:
Most chemistry happens in solvent, not in vacuum. Implicit solvation models replace the discrete solvent with a polarizable continuum characterized by its dielectric constant ε. The solute sits in a cavity carved into this continuum; surface charges on the cavity respond to the solute's electrostatic potential, and the solute responds to the surface charges — solved self-consistently.

The Polarizable Continuum Model (PCM) family (Tomasi and collaborators) is the most common implementation. IEFPCM (Integral Equation Formalism PCM) is the modern variant; CPCM is a conductor-like simplification often used for quick estimates. COSMO (Klamt) and its refinement COSMO-RS use a conductor-like cavity and add statistical thermodynamics for activity coefficients and partition coefficients. SMD (Truhlar) is parameterized for solvation free energies and is the standard for chemical accuracy ΔG_solv (mean errors ~1 kcal/mol for neutrals, ~4 kcal/mol for ions).

Implicit models capture electrostatics and bulk dielectric response well but miss specific solute-solvent interactions: hydrogen bonds, halogen bonds, π-stacking with solvent. For these you need a few explicit solvent molecules (cluster-continuum) or a full QM/MM treatment.

concepts.title: QM/MM and Hybrid Approaches
concepts.contentHtml:
For enzymes, materials interfaces, and bulk-solvent effects on chemistry, the answer is QM/MM (Warshel and Levitt, 1976; Nobel Prize 2013). Treat the chemically active region (active site, reactant, transition-state region) at the QM level — DFT or higher — and the surroundings (protein, solvent) with a classical molecular mechanics force field (AMBER, CHARMM, OPLS). The two regions interact electrostatically and (in subtractive schemes) through bonded terms.

Two main flavors. Additive QM/MM: write the energy as E_QM + E_MM + E_QM/MM, where the coupling term includes electrostatic embedding (MM point charges polarize the QM density) and van der Waals. Subtractive QM/MM, of which ONIOM (Morokuma) is the most popular variant, defines E = E_full,low + E_small,high − E_small,low; cleaner conceptually, but sensitive to the boundary treatment.

The boundary between QM and MM regions is the hard part — covalent bonds straddling the boundary need link atoms (capping H atoms) or specialized boundary-atom approaches. Done right, QM/MM lets you study the full energetics of an enzymatic reaction with DFT-quality electronic structure on the active site and a realistic protein environment for everything else. Most modern enzyme mechanism papers use it.

concepts.title: The Software Landscape
concepts.contentHtml:
The codes shape the field. Gaussian (Pople and others, since 1970) is the historical default — full-featured, well-documented, expensive license, closed source. ORCA (Neese, Max Planck, free for academia) has overtaken Gaussian in many groups thanks to fast DLPNO-CCSD(T), excellent multireference (NEVPT2, DLPNO-NEVPT2), and active development. Psi4 (Sherrill, open source) is Python-scriptable, popular for method development. Q-Chem (Head-Gordon and others) is strong on excited-state methods.

Solid-state and periodic codes — VASP, Quantum ESPRESSO, CP2K, FHI-aims — use plane waves or numeric atomic orbitals and serve materials science. They overlap with molecular codes only at the GGA/hybrid-DFT level. NWChem and MOLPRO remain active for high-end multireference work.

Reproducibility matters more than ever. Always report: program name and version, method (functional + basis), solvation model, optimization criteria, frequency scaling, dispersion correction, integration grid (for DFT — "ultrafine" or "M4" or whatever the code calls its dense option). The FAIR principles (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable) and tools like ioChem-BD push computational chemistry toward sharing the actual input/output files alongside the paper.

title: Machine-Learned Potentials and the ML-DFT Era
description: ANI, MACE, Allegro, ML-corrected DFT — the new shape of computational chemistry

concepts.title: Neural Network Potentials: ANI, SchNet, MACE
concepts.contentHtml:
A machine-learned potential (MLP) learns the potential energy surface from a database of ab initio calculations and predicts E(R) and forces in milliseconds — orders of magnitude faster than DFT. Train on enough configurations and the MLP reproduces DFT-quality energies for systems within its training distribution.

Three generations roughly track the field. ANI-1x / ANI-2x (Roitberg, 2018-2020) uses Behler-Parrinello atom-centered descriptors and dense feedforward networks; trained on millions of organic molecule snapshots, it nearly matches ωB97X/6-31G(d) on small organics for ~10⁵ × the speed. SchNet (Schütt, 2017) introduced continuous-filter convolutional layers acting on interatomic distances. MACE (Batatia, 2022) and Allegro (Musaelian, 2023) use equivariant message-passing with E(3)-symmetric tensor representations, achieving DFT accuracy on materials with much smaller training sets and with strict rotational/translational equivariance built into the architecture.

The current frontier is foundation models: a single large MLP trained across the periodic table on millions of DFT calculations, intended to generalize to chemistry it has never seen. MACE-MP-0 (2023) and the OMat24-trained successors are early examples — they're not as accurate as a system-specific MLP, but they cover most of chemistry out of the box.
mathExpressions: \text{ANI training cost: millions of DFT snapshots; inference: } \sim 10^{-3} \text{ s / molecule}

concepts.title: Active Learning and Transfer Learning
concepts.contentHtml:
An MLP is only as good as its training set. The danger is extrapolation: the model sees a configuration it didn't train on and confidently outputs nonsense. Active learning closes the loop: train a model, run molecular dynamics, monitor an uncertainty estimate (variance across an ensemble of models, or distance from training data in feature space), and trigger a fresh DFT calculation whenever the uncertainty exceeds a threshold. Add the new datapoint to the training set, retrain, repeat.

Done well, this generates a training set that's just big enough to cover the configurations the simulation actually visits — typically a few thousand DFT calculations rather than the millions of pre-built sets like ANI. Active-learning frameworks include FLARE (Vandermause), PLUMED-MLP integrations, and MACE's built-in uncertainty estimation.

Δ-learning trains an MLP to predict the difference between a cheap method (e.g., GFN2-xTB) and an expensive one (e.g., DLPNO-CCSD(T)). The cheap method handles most of the physics; the MLP only has to learn the residual. This trick gets you closer to high-level accuracy with much less training data — a practical win for catalysis and reaction barriers.

concepts.title: ML-Corrected DFT and the Honest Outlook
concepts.contentHtml:
The most consequential ML development inside DFT itself is machine-learned exchange-correlation functionals. DM21 (DeepMind, 2021) uses a neural network to evaluate a meta-GGA-style functional, trained on a curated set of high-accuracy reference data plus exact-condition constraints. It produces noticeably better energies on systems where standard functionals fail (radicals, charge-transfer, transition states) without sacrificing performance elsewhere.

The catch: these functionals are not yet broadly deployed in production codes, and the field is wary — an opaque neural network inside a quantum-mechanical calculation is hard to debug. The next decade will tell whether ML functionals replace human-designed ones or supplement them. Either way, the line between "DFT" and "ML potential" is blurring fast.

The honest outlook for quantum chemistry in 2026: DFT remains the workhorse for routine work. CCSD(T) is the gold standard but pricey. Multireference methods (NEVPT2, DMRG, CASSCF) handle hard cases. ML potentials handle dynamics and screening at orders-of-magnitude lower cost. ML-corrected DFT improves accuracy at no additional cost. The field is no longer a single pipeline — it's a toolkit, and the skill is in choosing the right combination for the problem at hand.
mathExpressions: \text{accuracy/cost frontier shifts with each generation of ML methods}
